messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 36
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Detective
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 74

He is nine years old when the kitchen first becomes a minefield. The scent of burnt cumin and his mother’s brass spice tines still catches him off guard, dragging him back to the linoleum floor, the heavy thud of a leather belt, the way the ceiling fan clicks with every rotation, counting down the seconds until it stops. He learns quickly to read the house like a crime scene. Footsteps on the stairs dictate his movements. The slam of a cabinet door signals a shift in the air. Survival becomes an exercise in prediction, a quiet calibration of footsteps, tone, and timing. He carries that early training into his work as a detective. At thirty-six, he is drawn to the orderly logic of case files, evidence boards, and witness statements. The job makes sense to him. Questions have answers. Patterns reveal truth. But the very skills that keep him sharp also keep him trapped in the past. On the stand, when a suspect’s voice drops into a familiar, guttural register, his chest constricts. During shift changes, the sudden wail of a siren sends his pulse racing for a full minute before he consciously tells himself it is just traffic. He wears his body armor like a second skin, but underneath, his nervous system remains permanently wound. He notices the tremor in a suspect’s hand, the slight shift in posture that signals deception, yet he also notices the way his own breath hitches when his supervisor raises his voice during a briefing. He stops mid-sentence, throat closing, and suddenly he is not in the precinct anymore. He is nine years old, counting the fan clicks. At home, he tries to be the steady presence his wife, Meera, needs. They have been married for eight years, and she knows his silences better than anyone. Still, there are moments when his distance feels like a glass wall. Last week, he wakes up gasping, convinced his bedroom door is being forced open. He finds himself standing in the hallway, eyes scanning for escape routes, before he registers Meera’s soft voice calling his name. He kisses her forehead and goes to the sink, but his hands shake so badly he spills hot water on his wrist. He does not feel the burn until later. During the day, he pushes through double shifts, cataloging details others miss, but the weight accumulates. He stops leaving his phone charging in the bedroom. He double-checks the deadbolt three times before bed. He learns to move through his own life as if he is defusing a device. Today, he leans forward, elbows on his knees, and describes a case from yesterday. A juvenile suspect kicks a metal desk in rage. The sound echoes like a gunshot. His pen snaps in his hand. He walks out of the interview room, steps into the stairwell, and counts backward from ten until the ringing in his ears stops. He comes back every Tuesday. He brings a worn leather notebook filled with sketches of crime scene layouts, but lately, the pages are filled with fragmented memories, drawn in careful, trembling lines. He says he is learning to breathe through the static. He says he is trying to stay. He sits in the chair now, waiting for the next session, his hands resting calmly on his thighs, the overhead fan turning in slow, steady circles.
